question: Harshavardhana ascended the throne of Thaneswar and Kanauj in 606 AD at the young age of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is 16 years.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Harsha became king in 606 AD when he was only 16 years old, after the sudden death of his father and the murder of his elder brother (हर्षवर्धन का राज्याभिषेक — 606 ई., 16 वर्ष की आयु)

 

• He was the younger son of Prabhakaravardhana of the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) family, whose capital was Thaneswar.

 

• His elder brother Rajyavardhana was killed by Shashanka, the Gauda ruler, which pushed Harsha to the throne.

 

• Harsha later made Kanauj his capital and ruled until his death in 647 AD, so his reign lasted about forty-one years.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The year 606 AD is taken as the starting point of the Harsha era, which Indian tradition links with his accession.

 

• Harsha used the title Siladitya, a name also mentioned by Hiuen Tsang.

 

• Harsha's sister Rajyashri was the widow of the Maukhari ruler Grahavarman of Kanauj.

 

• Harsha is described in the notes as the last great Hindu emperor of north India.

 

NOTE

 

• 12 years (Option 1): Twelve years is too young for Harsha at accession, since the sources and the notes agree that he was sixteen when he took the throne of Thaneswar in 606 AD. He was sixteen,.

 

• 20 years (Option 3): Twenty years is above his actual age at accession. The notes and standard texts give sixteen, and he was the younger son of Prabhakaravardhana.

 

• 25 years (Option 4): Twenty-five years does not fit the record of a king who took the throne in 606 AD and died in 647 AD after a long reign of about four decades.

question: The Harshacharita, the first historical biography written in Sanskrit, was composed by the court poet of Harsha named:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Banabhatta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Harshacharita was written by Banabhatta (Bana), the court poet of Harshavardhana; it is regarded as the first historical biography in Sanskrit and a chief source on Harsha (बाणभट्ट — हर्षचरित)

 

• Bana also wrote the Sanskrit prose romance Kadambari, a landmark of classical Sanskrit literature.

 

• Along with the account of Hiuen Tsang, the Harshacharita is one of the two chief sources for the reign of Harsha.

 

• The work narrates the story of the Pushyabhuti family, the rise of Prabhakaravardhana and Harsha's accession.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Harshacharita has eight chapters called ucchvasas, the first few giving the autobiography of Bana himself.

 

• Harsha's own plays Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarsika are another literary source for his age.

 

• Bana belonged to a Brahmin family of Bihar origin and joined the court after meeting Harsha.

 

• Kadambari was left incomplete by Bana and finished by his son.

 

NOTE

 

• Kalidasa (Option 1): Kalidasa was the great Sanskrit poet and dramatist of the Gupta period, famous for Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghaduta. He lived long before Harsha and did not write a biography of him.

 

• Vishakhadatta (Option 2): Vishakhadatta wrote the political drama Mudrarakshasa about Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya. He is not associated with the court or biography of Harsha.

 

• Rajashekhara (Option 3): Rajashekhara was a poet of the Gurjara-Pratihara court at Kannauj, author of Karpuramanjari and Kavyamimamsa. He belongs to a later age than Harsha.

question: The Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang, who visited India during the reign of Harsha, wrote his travel account under the title:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Si-Yu-Ki.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Hiuen Tsang's famous travelogue is Si-Yu-Ki (Records of the Western World), written after his stay in India in the seventh century during the reign of Harsha (सी-यू-की — ह्वेनसांग का यात्रा-वृत्तांत)

 

• His account gives details of Harsha's administration, the religious assemblies at Kanauj and Prayag, and Buddhist centres such as Nalanda.

 

• Hiuen Tsang is also called the Prince of Pilgrims, and Harsha welcomed him with great honour.

 

• The Si-Yu-Ki and the Harshacharita of Bana are the two principal sources for the history of Harsha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hiuen Tsang studied at Nalanda and returned to China with many Buddhist manuscripts.

 

• Fa-Hien came earlier, in the time of the Gupta ruler Chandragupta II.

 

• Harsha's Prayag gathering held every five years is known mainly from Hiuen Tsang's description.

 

• The Harshacharita adds to the Chinese account with a courtly Indian viewpoint.

 

NOTE

 

• Kitab-ul-Hind (Option 2): Kitab-ul-Hind was written by the Arab-Persian scholar Alberuni in the eleventh century about India, not by the Chinese traveller who visited Harsha.

 

• Rihla (Option 3): Rihla is the travel account of the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who came to India in the fourteenth century in the Tughlaq period.

 

• Fo-Kuo-Ki (Option 4): Fo-Kuo-Ki is the travel record of the Chinese monk Fa-Hien, who came in the Gupta age. It is not the work of Hiuen Tsang.

question: Which of the following is NOT a play written by Harshavardhana?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kadambari.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kadambari is a prose romance by Banabhatta, not a play by Harsha; Harsha himself wrote the plays Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarsika (कादंबरी — बाणभट्ट की रचना, हर्ष की नहीं)

 

• Harsha was not only a conqueror but also a literary man, and his three Sanskrit plays are valuable sources for the history of his age.

 

• Bana, the court poet, wrote two major works, the Harshacharita and Kadambari.

 

• Because the stem is a NOT-type question, the work that belongs to another author is the answer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ratnavali is a romantic comedy about King Udayana and Ratnavali.

 

• Nagananda has a Buddhist theme and tells of the self-sacrifice of Jimutavahana.

 

• Priyadarsika is another court romance connected with Udayana.

 

• Kadambari was completed after Bana's death by his son Bhushanabhatta.

 

• Ratnavali and Priyadarsika are light court romances, whereas Nagananda carries the Buddhist ideal of self-sacrifice. With the prose of Bana, they make Harsha's age one of the richest periods of Sanskrit literature after the Gupta era.

 

NOTE

 

• Ratnavali (Option 1): Ratnavali is one of the three plays composed by Harsha himself. Since it is genuinely his work, it cannot be the exception in a NOT question.

 

• Nagananda (Option 2): Nagananda is a Sanskrit play by Harsha with a Buddhist story of Jimutavahana. As it is his own composition, it cannot be the correct answer here.

 

• Priyadarsika (Option 4): Priyadarsika is a romantic play attributed to Harsha, one of the three named in the notes. It is therefore not the odd one out.

question: In which year (AD) did the king Harshavardhana die?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 647.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Harshavardhana died in 647 AD after a reign of about forty-one years; his death marked the end of his empire and renewed political fragmentation in north India (हर्षवर्धन की मृत्यु — 647 ई.)

 

• He had ruled since 606 AD, so the span 606-647 AD is the period of the Vardhana ascendancy at Kanauj.

 

• He left no strong successor, and his large kingdom, which depended on his personal ability, broke up soon after.

 

• After him, north India was divided among many regional dynasties, including the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas and Rajput clans.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hiuen Tsang left India a few years before Harsha's death, having stayed in the country for about fifteen years.

 

• The decades after 647 AD saw Kanauj contested by several regional powers.

 

• Harsha is called the last great Hindu emperor of north India.

 

• The Harsha era is counted from 606 AD.

 

NOTE

 

• 550 (Option 1): 550 AD falls in the late Gupta period, long before Harsha came to the throne in 606 AD. It cannot be the year of his death.

 

• 783 (Option 3): 783 AD is in the age of the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas, well after Harsha. His reign ended about 136 years earlier.

 

• 829 (Option 4): 829 AD belongs to the period of Pala king Devapala and the early Pratihara rulers. Harsha had been dead for almost two centuries by then.

question: According to the Aihole inscription, which ruler defeated Harsha when he tried to extend his kingdom south of the Narmada?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pulakesin II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Aihole inscription records that Pulakesin II of the Western Chalukya dynasty defeated Harsha, who wished to expand south of the Narmada, and Pulakesin then took the title Paramesvara (ऐहोल अभिलेख — पुलकेशिन द्वितीय की जीत)

 

• This was Harsha's most important campaign and also one of the few reverses of his career, which fixed the Narmada as the southern limit of his realm.

 

• The inscription was composed by the court poet Ravikirti in the Chalukya capital area of Badami (Vatapi) and dates to about 634 AD.

 

• Pulakesin II became the strongest power of the Deccan after this victory.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pulakesin II also defeated the Pallava king Mahendravarman I but was later defeated by Narasimhavarman I.

 

• Aihole in Karnataka is famous for its early temples built by the Chalukyas.

 

• The Chalukya capital was Vatapi (modern Badami).

 

• Harsha's kingdom thus did not extend into the Deccan.

 

• Pulakesin II's power later suffered when the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I attacked Vatapi in about 642 AD, so the Aihole record of 634 AD marks the peak of Chalukya authority in the Deccan.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahendravarman I (Option 1): Mahendravarman I was a Pallava king of Kanchipuram who himself lost to Pulakesin II. The Aihole inscription names the Chalukya king as the victor over Harsha, not him.

 

• Dhruva (Option 2): Dhruva was a Rashtrakuta ruler of the eighth century who fought for Kanauj against the Pratiharas and Palas. He lived long after Harsha.

 

• Dharmapala (Option 4): Dharmapala was a Pala king of Bengal in the late eighth century. He was not a contemporary of Harsha and has no link with the Aihole inscription.

question:
Consider the following statements:

1. Harshavardhana himself wrote the Harshacharita.

2. Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarsika are plays composed by Harsha.

3. Banabhatta was the court poet of Harsha.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The true statements here are 2 and 3: Harsha wrote the plays Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarsika, and Banabhatta was his court poet; statement 1 is wrong because the Harshacharita was written by Bana (हर्ष के नाटक — रत्नावली, नागानंद, प्रियदर्शिका)

 

• The Harshacharita is a biography of Harsha and was composed by a court poet, not by the king himself.

 

• Harsha's plays are useful for understanding court life and his religious outlook, as Nagananda reflects a Buddhist theme.

 

• The correct combination therefore keeps the plays and the court poet, and drops the mistaken authorship of the biography.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bana also wrote Kadambari, one of the finest Sanskrit prose romances.

 

• The Harshacharita is accepted as the first historical biography in Sanskrit.

 

• Hiuen Tsang's account is the main foreign source for Harsha.

 

• Harsha's plays are in Sanskrit and are courtly in tone.

 

• Harsha's own copper plate grants, such as those of Madhuban and Banskhera, record his genealogy and land gifts, and they confirm the family details given in Bana's Harshacharita, so the king's records support his court poet.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): This combination includes statement 1, which wrongly credits Harsha with writing the Harshacharita, and it leaves out statement 3. Bana was the court poet and the author of that biography, so statement 1 fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): This combination also keeps the false statement 1 while dropping statement 2. Harsha really did compose the plays Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarsika, so statement 2 must be included and statement 1 excluded.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This combination claims that all three statements are true, which is wrong because statement 1 makes Harsha the author of the Harshacharita. That work was composed by the poet Bana.

question:
Consider the following statements about the religious assembly held at Kanauj under Harsha:

1. It was organised to honour the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang.

2. Representatives of every religious sect were invited.

3. It was held at the very beginning of Harsha's reign, before his conquests.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Kanauj assembly question, statements 1 and 2 are right: Harsha organised the Kanauj assembly to honour Hiuen Tsang and invited representatives of every religious sect, but it was held towards the close of his reign, not at its beginning (कन्नौज सभा — ह्वेनसांग के सम्मान में)

 

• The assembly shows Harsha's religious tolerance and his respect for the Chinese visitor, whose account preserves the details.

 

• By the time of the assembly Harsha was already master of a large kingdom with Kanauj as capital, so statement 3 contradicts the record.

 

• The gathering is often called the Kanauj Assembly and is distinct from the quinquennial gathering at Prayag.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kanauj was made the new capital by Harsha, which raised him to the most powerful ruler of north India.

 

• Hiuen Tsang had studied at Nalanda before the assembly.

 

• Harsha was personally inclined to Buddhism in later life while honouring Hindu gods too.

 

• Kanauj later became the prize of the tripartite struggle among Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This combination drops statement 1 and includes the false statement 3. The assembly was held towards the close of the reign to honour Hiuen Tsang, so statement 1 is true and statement 3 is false.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): This combination pairs statement 1 with the false statement 3 and leaves out statement 2. Representatives of all sects were invited, so statement 2 is true and must be included.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This combination says all three are true, which fails because statement 3 places the assembly at the start of the reign. In fact it came near the end of Harsha's rule.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Prayag (Allahabad) assembly described by Hiuen Tsang:

1. It was one of the gatherings that Harsha held routinely every five years.

2. Harsha gave away his enormous wealth as gifts to members of all religious sects.

3. Hiuen Tsang says Harsha emptied the treasury and even gave away his own clothes and jewels.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: the Prayag assembly was held every five years, Harsha distributed his wealth to all religious sects, and according to Hiuen Tsang he even gave away his own clothes and jewels (प्रयाग सभा — हर्ष का पंचवार्षिक दान)

 

• The gathering took place at Prayag, the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna, a place sacred to Hindus.

 

• The generosity described reveals the wealth of the royal treasury and Harsha's religious liberality towards Buddhists, Brahmins and others.

 

• Since the account comes from a foreign eye-witness, it is taken as reliable evidence of the practice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The assembly is also known as the Mahamoksha Parishad in later accounts.

 

• Prayag is the modern Prayagraj in Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Harsha reportedly took a simple garment from his sister after giving everything away.

 

• Gift-giving to all sects reflects the religious tolerance of the Vardhana ruler.

 

• Hiuen Tsang says Harsha divided his income into four parts, for state expenses, for officials, for scholars and for religious gifts. This shows how central charity was in his reign, apart from the Prayag distributions.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): This combination keeps only statements 1 and 2 and ignores the third. The remark that Harsha emptied the treasury and gave away even his clothes is also recorded, so statement 3 is true.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This combination omits statement 1 although the five-yearly nature of the gathering is stated in the account. Statement 1 is true and must be counted.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): This combination leaves out statement 2 although the gifts to all sects are the main point of the account. Statement 2 is true, so the answer must include all three.

question:
Match the following:

(a) Harshacharita  (i) Hiuen Tsang

(b) Si-Yu-Ki  (ii) Ravikirti

(c) Aihole inscription  (iii) Banabhatta

(d) Nagananda  (iv) Harsha
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct pairs are Harshacharita - Banabhatta, Si-Yu-Ki - Hiuen Tsang, Aihole inscription - Ravikirti and Nagananda - Harsha, which gives a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv (स्रोत और रचनाकार का मेल)

 

• Harshacharita and Si-Yu-Ki are the two chief sources for Harsha's reign, one Indian and one Chinese.

 

• The Aihole inscription was composed by Ravikirti to record the victories of Pulakesin II, including the defeat of Harsha.

 

• Nagananda is one of the three plays of Harsha, along with Ratnavali and Priyadarsika.

 

• The pairing of Indian and foreign sources is a common SSC pattern: literary works give the court view, inscriptions give dated political facts, and the travelogue gives an outsider's description of society and religion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ravikirti was the court poet of the Chalukya king Pulakesin II.

 

• Banabhatta also wrote Kadambari.

 

• Hiuen Tsang's book is the Records of the Western World.

 

• Harsha's plays are in Sanskrit.

 

• Ravikirti's Aihole prashasti is a Sanskrit eulogy in verse engraved on the Meguti temple at Aihole and dated Saka 556 (634 AD), which makes it a precisely dated source for the politics of the Deccan in Harsha's age.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-iv, d-ii (Option 1): This combination pairs the Harshacharita with Hiuen Tsang and Si-Yu-Ki with Banabhatta, which reverses the authors. The Harshacharita is by Bana and Si-Yu-Ki by the Chinese pilgrim.

 

• a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i (Option 2): This combination gives the Harshacharita to Ravikirti and Nagananda to Hiuen Tsang, which is wrong. Ravikirti composed the Aihole inscription and Nagananda is Harsha's own play.

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 3): This combination links Si-Yu-Ki with Ravikirti and the Aihole inscription with Hiuen Tsang. Both pairs are wrong, as the inscription belongs to Ravikirti and the travel book to the pilgrim.

question: Harsha's father, regarded as the real founder of Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) power with his capital at Thaneswar, was:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Prabhakaravardhana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Prabhakaravardhana is regarded as the real founder of the Pushyabhuti or Vardhana greatness; his capital was Thaneswar, north of Delhi, and his sons were Rajyavardhana and Harsha (प्रभाकरवर्धन — थानेश्वर का शासक)

 

• The Pushyabhutis had earlier been feudatories of the Guptas, and after the Gupta decline they rose as an independent power.

 

• His elder son Rajyavardhana succeeded him but was killed soon after, which brought Harsha to the throne in 606 AD.

 

• His daughter Rajyashri was married to Grahavarman of the Maukhari family of Kanauj.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Thaneswar in Haryana was later also the capital before Harsha shifted to Kanauj.

 

• After Gupta decline north India fell into disunity until the early seventh century.

 

• Harsha's kingdom grew out of the Thaneswar-Kanauj union.

 

• The Pushyabhutis called themselves Vardhanas.

 

• After Rajyavardhana was killed by Shashanka of Gauda, Harsha first rescued his widowed sister Rajyashri in the Vindhya forest, as the Harshacharita records, and then took charge of the Maukhari kingdom of Kanauj.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajyavardhana (Option 2): Rajyavardhana was Harsha's elder brother and Prabhakaravardhana's son. He ruled only briefly and was killed, so he is not the founder or the father asked about.

 

• Grahavarman (Option 3): Grahavarman was the Maukhari king of Kanauj who married Rajyashri, Harsha's sister. He was a brother-in-law of Harsha and not his father.

 

• Shashanka (Option 4): Shashanka was the Gauda ruler of Bengal who is blamed for the death of Rajyavardhana. He was an enemy of the family and not its founder.

question:
Assertion (A): Harshavardhana made Kanauj his new capital, which made him the most powerful ruler in north India.

Reason (R): Thaneswar, the earlier capital of the Pushyabhutis, lay to the north of Delhi.

Choose the correct option.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true but R does not explain A: Harsha shifted the capital to Kanauj, the political centre of north India, while Thaneswar, the earlier seat, was simply a location north of Delhi (हर्ष की राजधानी — थानेश्वर से कन्नौज)

 

• The position of Thaneswar is only a geographical fact and gives no reason why Kanauj became more powerful.

 

• Kanauj gave Harsha a central position in the Gangetic plain, and the Maukhari connection through his sister made its control natural.

 

• After Harsha, the contest for Kanauj continued in the tripartite struggle of Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kanauj had been the Maukhari capital before Harsha.

 

• Thaneswar is in present-day Haryana.

 

• The importance of Kanauj lasted until the Rajput period.

 

• Harsha's court at Kanauj hosted Hiuen Tsang.

 

• Thaneswar (Sthanvishvara) lies near the sacred land of Kurukshetra and was the seat of the Pushyabhutis before 606 AD, which is why the family is also called the Thaneswar line of the Vardhanas.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This choice says R is the correct explanation of A, which is wrong. The location of Thaneswar north of Delhi does not explain why Kanauj made Harsha powerful.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): This choice calls A true but R false, which is wrong. Thaneswar was indeed located north of Delhi, so R is a true statement.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): This choice calls A false, which is wrong. Harsha did make Kanauj his new capital and it raised his standing in north India.

question:
Assertion (A): The account of Hiuen Tsang is regarded as an important source for the history of Harsha.

Reason (R): Hiuen Tsang visited India during Harsha's reign and recorded his observations in Si-Yu-Ki.

Choose the correct option.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both A and R are true and R explains A: Hiuen Tsang was an eyewitness who came during Harsha's reign and wrote Si-Yu-Ki, so his book is a chief source on Harsha (प्रत्यक्षदर्शी विवरण — ह्वेनसांग)

 

• A contemporary foreign visitor is valuable because he records the administration, religion and society of the period without court bias.

 

• His account is used together with Bana's Harshacharita to cross-check events.

 

• The pilgrim also describes the Prayag gathering and the Kanauj assembly held in his honour.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hiuen Tsang is also known as Xuanzang.

 

• His book was translated into European languages in the nineteenth century.

 

• Harsha's court received the pilgrim with great honour.

 

• His stay at Nalanda is described in his biography.

 

• Alongside Hiuen Tsang, Bana's Harshacharita is the chief Indian literary source and Harsha's plays add a third view. Historians check the Chinese pilgrim's statements against these Sanskrit works to separate court praise from observed fact.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This choice says R is not an explanation of A, which is wrong. The fact that he visited during the reign and recorded it is exactly why his account is a source.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): This choice treats R as false, which is wrong. Hiuen Tsang did visit in the seventh century in Harsha's reign and he did write Si-Yu-Ki.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): This choice treats A as false, which is wrong. The Chinese pilgrim's account is accepted as a major source for Harsha.

question:
Consider the following statements about Hiuen Tsang:

1. He came to India in the seventh century AD.

2. He wrote the book Indica.

3. Harsha organised an assembly at Kanauj to honour him.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Of the three statements, 1 and 3 hold good: Hiuen Tsang came in the seventh century and Harsha honoured him with the Kanauj assembly; statement 2 is wrong because Indica was written by Megasthenes (ह्वेनसांग — सातवीं शताब्दी, कन्नौज सभा)

 

• Hiuen Tsang's own work is Si-Yu-Ki, a record of what he saw in India and Central Asia.

 

• Indica belongs to the Mauryan period and describes the court of Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• The question therefore tests whether one can separate the Chinese traveller of Harsha's age from the Greek ambassador of the Mauryas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus I Nicator.

 

• Fa-Hien visited in the Gupta age, earlier than Hiuen Tsang.

 

• Hiuen Tsang studied at Nalanda under the teacher Silabhadra.

 

• Harsha also hosted him at Prayag.

 

• Hiuen Tsang describes Nalanda as a great monastery with thousands of monks and teachers, supported by the revenue of many villages, and he studied there under the teacher Silabhadra before returning to China.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): This combination includes the false statement 2 and leaves out statement 3. Hiuen Tsang did not write Indica, and the Kanauj assembly was held in his honour.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This combination also keeps the false statement 2 but drops statement 1. He did come in the seventh century, so statement 1 must be counted.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This combination says all three are true, but statement 2 is false because Indica was written by the Greek ambassador Megasthenes.

question:
Consider the following statements about Harsha's campaigns:

1. He defeated Dhruvasena II of Valabhi, who then became his vassal.

2. His campaign against Pulakesin II ended in his defeat.

3. He was victorious over the Western Chalukya ruler Pulakesin II on the Narmada.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Two statements, 1 and 2, are accurate: Dhruvasena II of Valabhi was defeated and became a vassal, while the campaign against Pulakesin II failed; statement 3 reverses the result (हर्ष के अभियान — वल्लभी पर विजय, पुलकेशिन से पराजय)

 

• The Aihole inscription records Harsha's defeat and the title Paramesvara taken by Pulakesin II afterwards.

 

• Harsha's wish to extend his kingdom south of the Narmada was therefore checked, and the river became his southern frontier.

 

• Valabhi in Gujarat was an important western state, and its submission extended his influence towards the Arabian Sea.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Valabhi was the capital of the Maitraka dynasty.

 

• According to many accounts Dhruvasena II later married Harsha's daughter.

 

• Harsha's last campaign was against Kalinga.

 

• Pulakesin II ruled from Vatapi.

 

• The Aihole inscription is dated Saka 556 (634 AD), so Harsha's defeat must be placed before that year, while his campaign against Kalinga came later, at about 643 AD, as the last major war of his reign.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This combination drops statement 1 and includes statement 3. Valabhi's submission is recorded, and statement 3 wrongly claims a victory over Pulakesin II.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This combination includes statement 3 and omits statement 2, but statement 3 is the false one because Harsha lost to Pulakesin.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): This combination calls all three statements true, but statement 3 contradicts statement 2 and the Aihole record of Harsha's defeat.

question: The Valabhi ruler Dhruvasena II, who was defeated by Harsha and became his vassal, ruled over a kingdom located in:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gujarat (Saurashtra).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Valabhi, ruled by the Maitraka king Dhruvasena II, lay in Gujarat (Saurashtra), and after defeat he became a vassal of Harsha (वल्लभी — गुजरात/सौराष्ट्र)

 

• Valabhi was a rich trading state of western India and later became a famous centre of learning, comparable to Nalanda.

 

• The submission of Valabhi extended Harsha's power towards the western coast.

 

• The notes list this victory among Harsha's early successes in building a large kingdom after the Gupta decline.

 

• For SSC, remember the direction of each Harsha campaign: west against Valabhi, south against Pulakesin II (failure) and east against Kalinga (success), because questions often ask which campaign succeeded or failed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Many accounts say Harsha gave a daughter in marriage to Dhruvasena II.

 

• Valabhi was later destroyed after Arab raids in the eighth century.

 

• The Maitrakas ruled from the sixth to the eighth century.

 

• Bana's Harshacharita refers to the west Indian campaigns.

 

• Valabhi's wealth came from the sea trade of the western ports, and Hiuen Tsang notes its many Buddhist monasteries, which helps explain why Harsha wanted its alliance and submission in the west.

 

NOTE

 

• Bengal (Option 1): Bengal was the territory of the Gauda ruler Shashanka, Harsha's rival, and later of the Palas and Senas. Valabhi was not in that region.

 

• Kamarupa (Assam) (Option 2): Kamarupa in Assam was ruled by Bhaskaravarman, who was an ally of Harsha and not a defeated vassal. Valabhi was not there.

 

• Kashmir (Option 4): Kashmir was under the Karkota dynasty in this period and is far from the Saurashtra coast. It has no link with Dhruvasena II.

question: Which of the following regions was NOT under the rule of Harshavardhana?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tamil Nadu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tamil Nadu was never part of Harsha's kingdom; his southward drive was stopped at the Narmada by Pulakesin II, while north Indian regions such as Punjab, Bihar and Orissa were under his control (हर्ष का साम्राज्य — उत्तर भारत तक सीमित)

 

• Harsha's last campaign against Kalinga in Orissa succeeded, and the notes record that Rajasthan, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Orissa were under his direct control.

 

• The far south was ruled by the Pallavas, Cholas, Pandyas and Cheras, and the Deccan by the Chalukyas.

 

• Because the stem is a NOT-type, the region lying beyond his limits is the answer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pallavas of Kanchipuram ruled Tamil Nadu in Harsha's age.

 

• Harsha's kingdom was mainly in the Gangetic plain and the north.

 

• The Narmada marked the line between the north and the Deccan in his time.

 

• Kanauj stood at the centre of his realm.

 

• Harsha's empire was less centralised than the Mauryan or Gupta state: many feudatory chiefs, called samantas, kept their own armies and territories while acknowledging him as overlord, which made it fragile after his death.

 

NOTE

 

• Punjab (Option 1): Punjab is listed in the notes among the areas under Harsha's direct control. Since it was part of his kingdom, it cannot be the exception.

 

• Bihar (Option 3): Bihar was held by Harsha and contained great Buddhist centres such as Nalanda in his age. It is not the region outside his rule.

 

• Orissa (Option 4): Orissa came under Harsha after his successful last campaign against Kalinga. It was part of his empire, so it is not the answer.

question: Who is regarded as the founder of the Pala dynasty in Bengal?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gopala.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Gopala founded the Pala dynasty around 750 AD in Bengal after being chosen by the local chiefs to end the prevailing disorder (गोपाल — पाल वंश के संस्थापक, 750 ई.)

 

• The Palas were dominant in the Bengal region from the mid-8th to the 12th century, ruling Bengal and Bihar.

 

• Gopala also founded the Odantapuri university in Bihar, which was later destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji.

 

• His son Dharmapala (770-810 AD) raised the Pala kingdom to a major power.

 

• The Pala accession is described as an election by the leading men of Bengal, a rare event in Indian history that ended a long period of disorder and made Gopala the first king of a dynasty lasting four centuries.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Palas were Buddhists and patronised Buddhist learning.

 

• The period before Gopala was one of anarchy in Bengal, called matsyanyaya.

 

• The Palas took part in the tripartite struggle for Kanauj.

 

• Madanapala is named in the notes as the last Pala ruler.

 

• Dharmapala, the son of Gopala, took the imperial titles Paramesvara Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja and installed his own nominee Chakrayudha on the throne of Kanauj, showing how fast Pala power grew after the founder.

 

NOTE

 

• Dharmapala (Option 1): Dharmapala was the son and successor of Gopala, who ruled from about 770 to 810 AD. He expanded the kingdom but was not its founder.

 

• Devapala (Option 2): Devapala was the son of Dharmapala and a later Pala ruler who fought at Kanauj. He was the third in the line and not the founder.

 

• Mahipala (Option 4): Mahipala I of the Pala line revived the kingdom later, in the eleventh century. He was not the first king of the Palas.

question: The famous Buddhist university at Vikramashila was founded by which Pala ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dharmapala.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty founded Vikramashila, a great Buddhist monastery-university in Bihar, and also revived Nalanda (धर्मपाल — विक्रमशिला विश्वविद्यालय)

 

• Dharmapala ruled from about 770 to 810 AD and was the son of Gopala, the founder of the dynasty.

 

• He was defeated by the Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva in the struggle for Kanauj, though the Palas remained powerful.

 

• Vikramashila became a leading centre of Vajrayana Buddhism and attracted scholars from Tibet.

 

• Vikramashila lay in the Bhagalpur region of Bihar on the Ganga, had many colleges and teachers, and was an important centre for Buddhist Tantric studies during the Pala period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dharmapala is also credited with founding the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur in present-day Bangladesh.

 

• Vikramashila was located near Bhagalpur in Bihar.

 

• Bakhtiyar Khilji destroyed several Buddhist centres in Bihar around 1200 AD.

 

• Atisha Dipankara was a famous teacher of Vikramashila.

 

• Excavations at Antichak in Bhagalpur district have revealed the ruins of the Vikramashila monastery, with a large cruciform stupa at its centre, which confirms the literary descriptions of the great institution.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahipala (Option 1): Mahipala I was a later Pala king who revived the dynasty's power in the eleventh century. He did not found Vikramashila.

 

• Gopala (Option 2): Gopala, the founder of the dynasty, is credited with the Odantapuri university, not Vikramashila. The latter was a creation of his son.

 

• Devapala (Option 3): Devapala was the son of Dharmapala and expanded the kingdom, but the founding of Vikramashila is credited to his father.

question: Odantapuri University in Bihar, founded by the Pala ruler Gopala, was later destroyed by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bakhtiyar Khilji.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Odantapuri, founded by Gopala, was destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji, the Turkish commander who attacked the Buddhist centres of Bihar at the end of the twelfth century (ओदंतपुरी — बख्तियार खिलजी द्वारा नष्ट)

 

• The destruction of Odantapuri, Vikramashila and Nalanda ended the great era of Buddhist monastic learning in eastern India.

 

• These raids came after the decline of the Pala dynasty, whose power had earlier protected the monasteries.

 

• Odantapuri was located in Bihar in the Magadha region, close to Nalanda.

 

• The Turkish raids of about 1200 AD struck Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri one after another, and the sources record the loss of libraries and the flight of monks to Nepal and Tibet.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bakhtiyar Khilji was a general of Qutbuddin Aibak.

 

• He also overran Bengal and defeated the Sena king Lakshmanasena at Nadia.

 

• Vikramashila was founded by Dharmapala.

 

• Buddhist monks fled to Tibet and Nepal after the destruction.

 

• Odantapuri stood near present-day Bihar Sharif, and Tibetan tradition says the first Tibetan monastery, Samye, was modelled on it, which shows the influence of Pala-age Bihar on the Buddhism of Tibet.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahmud of Ghazni (Option 1): Mahmud of Ghazni raided north-western India and Somnath in the early eleventh century. He did not attack the Bihar universities.

 

• Muhammad Ghori (Option 2): Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain but the Bihar monasteries were attacked by his general, not by him personally.

 

• Qutbuddin Aibak (Option 4): Qutbuddin Aibak was the Delhi Sultanate's first ruler in 1206. The attack on the Bihar universities is credited to his general Bakhtiyar Khilji.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Pala dynasty:

1. Gopala founded the dynasty in about 750 AD.

2. Dharmapala was the son of Gopala.

3. The Palas were dominant in the Bengal region from the mid-8th to the 12th century.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: Gopala founded the Pala line in about 750 AD, Dharmapala was his son, and the dynasty dominated Bengal from the mid-8th to the 12th century (पाल वंश — गोपाल, धर्मपाल, 750-12वीं सदी)

 

• The Palas thus ruled for about four centuries, one of the longest dynastic spans in early medieval north India.

 

• Their power rested on the plains of Bengal and Bihar, with capitals at places such as Monghyr and Pataliputra in different reigns.

 

• They are remembered for Buddhist patronage, including the monastic universities of Odantapuri, Vikramashila and Nalanda.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Palas followed Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism.

 

• Pala art produced fine stone sculptures and bronzes.

 

• Ramapala is remembered in the Ramacharita of Sandhyakar Nandi.

 

• The Palas were succeeded in Bengal by the Senas.

 

• Pala sculptors produced black basalt images of Buddha and Tara and fine bronzes, and Dhiman and Vitapala are named artists of the school. Pala palm-leaf manuscript painting also influenced the art of Nepal and Tibet.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): Statement 3 is also correct, so an answer that leaves it out is incomplete. The Palas held the Bengal region from the mid-8th to the 12th century, so it cannot be left out.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Leaving out statement 1 is wrong, because the founding by Gopala in about 750 AD is correct. Leaving it out makes the choice incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): An answer without statement 2 is faulty, since Dharmapala was indeed the son of Gopala who ruled from about 770 to 810 AD. It must be counted.

question:
Consider the following statements:

1. Devapala was the son of Dharmapala.

2. The Palas ruled over Bengal and Bihar.

3. Dharmapala founded the Odantapuri University.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct choices are statements 1 and 2: Devapala was the son of Dharmapala, and the Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar; statement 3 is wrong because Odantapuri was founded by Gopala (देवपाल, धर्मपाल का पुत्र; ओदंतपुरी — गोपाल)

 

• Dharmapala is linked with Vikramashila, while Gopala is linked with Odantapuri.

 

• Devapala consolidated the Pala power and fought in the struggle for Kanauj with the Pratiharas, as the notes record.

 

• The three Pala rulers Gopala, Dharmapala and Devapala therefore form the early and strongest part of the dynasty.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Devapala ruled in the first half of the ninth century.

 

• Devapala is said to have permitted a ruler of the Sailendra dynasty of Suvarnadvipa to build a monastery at Nalanda.

 

• Nalanda was revived under Pala patronage.

 

• Madanapala is named in the notes as the last Pala ruler.

 

• Devapala ruled for about four decades in the first half of the ninth century, and the records of his reign claim that Pala influence reached as far as Assam and Odisha, which marks the height of the early dynasty.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This combination drops statement 1 and includes statement 3. Devapala was Dharmapala's son, and Odantapuri was founded by Gopala, so statement 3 is false.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This combination pairs statement 1 with the false statement 3 and omits the true statement 2. Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This combination claims all three are true, but statement 3 wrongly credits Dharmapala with Odantapuri. That university is attributed to Gopala.

question:
Match the Pala rulers with their descriptions:

(a) Gopala  (i) Son of Dharmapala

(b) Dharmapala  (ii) Founder of the dynasty

(c) Devapala  (iii) Founder of Vikramashila

(d) Madanapala  (iv) Last Pala ruler
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Gopala - founder of the dynasty, Dharmapala - founder of Vikramashila, Devapala - son of Dharmapala and Madanapala - last Pala ruler, i.e. a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv (पाल शासक — गोपाल, धर्मपाल, देवपाल, मदनपाल)

 

• Gopala established the Pala power in 750 AD and also founded Odantapuri.

 

• Dharmapala ruled 770-810 AD and built or revived major Buddhist centres, while Devapala continued his policy.

 

• The notes mention Madanapala as the last Pala ruler, bringing the dynasty to its end in the twelfth century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pala dynasty lasted from about 750 AD to the twelfth century.

 

• Vikramashila and Odantapuri were destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji's raids.

 

• Devapala fought Pratihara rulers at Kanauj.

 

• The Senas replaced the Palas in much of Bengal.

 

• Ramapala, a later Pala king, recovered Varendra in north Bengal after a revolt, and the poet Sandhyakar Nandi narrates this in the Ramacharita, a poem with a double meaning about the god Rama and the king.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i (Option 1): This combination makes Gopala the founder of Vikramashila and Dharmapala the founder of the dynasty, which reverses their roles. Gopala founded the dynasty in 750 AD and Dharmapala created Vikramashila.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii (Option 3): This combination calls Gopala the son of Dharmapala and Dharmapala the last ruler, which turns the chronology upside down. Gopala was the first king and father of Dharmapala, and Madanapala came last.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): This combination makes Gopala the last ruler and Madanapala the founder, again reversing the order of the dynasty. Gopala began the line in about 750 AD and Madanapala belongs to its closing phase.

question: The Pala king Dharmapala was defeated in the struggle for Kanauj by the Rashtrakuta ruler:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dhruva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dhruva, the Rashtrakuta ruler, defeated the Pala king Dharmapala during the contest for Kanauj, showing that the Rashtrakutas were active far in the north (ध्रुव — धर्मपाल का विजेता)

 

• Dharmapala (770-810 AD) was the son of Gopala and the founder of Vikramashila.

 

• Dhruva also fought the Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja, so he took part in the tripartite struggle against both northern powers.

 

• Despite the defeat, the Pala dynasty recovered and remained strong in Bengal and Bihar.

 

• The conflict with Dhruva explains why Dharmapala could not hold Kanauj permanently, even though he had placed his own nominee on its throne, since outside powers like the Rashtrakutas kept intervening.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The tripartite struggle for Kanauj lasted for about two centuries.

 

• Dhruva's successor Govinda III also marched to the north.

 

• The Rashtrakutas ruled from Manyakheta in the Deccan.

 

• Kanauj remained the symbol of imperial power in north India.

 

• Dhruva's son Govinda III continued the northern campaigns and, according to Rashtrakuta records, defeated both Dharmapala and Chakrayudha, so the Deccan power repeatedly reached the Gangetic plain in this period.

 

NOTE

 

• Dantidurga (Option 1): Dantidurga was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty in the mid-eighth century. He came earlier than Dhruva and is not recorded as the victor over Dharmapala.

 

• Krishna III (Option 2): Krishna III ruled the Rashtrakutas in the tenth century and fought the Cholas at Takkolam. He lived long after Dharmapala.

 

• Amoghavarsha (Option 3): Amoghavarsha was a Rashtrakuta king of the ninth century known for patronising literature and for a long reign. He is not the opponent of Dharmapala.

question: Which three major powers were involved in the Tripartite Struggle for control over Kannauj during the early medieval period in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, and Palas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj was fought among the Gurjara-Pratiharas of the west, the Palas of the east and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan (त्रिपक्षीय संघर्ष — प्रतिहार, पाल, राष्ट्रकूट)

 

• Kannauj was the prize because control of it gave claim to the imperial status once held by Harsha.

 

• The struggle began in the eighth century and lasted for about two centuries without a permanent winner.

 

• It weakened all three powers and prepared the way for the rise of regional Rajput kingdoms.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dharmapala of the Palas and Vatsaraja of the Pratiharas were early rivals.

 

• Nagabhata II of the Pratiharas captured Kanauj.

 

• Mihir Bhoj of the Pratiharas later held Kanauj as capital.

 

• Devapala of the Palas also fought for Kanauj.

 

• Kannauj was a rich city on the Ganga in the doab and a symbol of imperial power since Harsha's time. None of the three powers held it for long, and the Gahadavalas later ruled it in the eleventh century.

 

NOTE

 

• Pallavas, Chalukyas, and Satavahanas (Option 2): Pallavas, Chalukyas and Satavahanas were south Indian and Deccan dynasties of different periods. They were not parties to the contest for Kannauj.

 

• Paramaras, Chauhans, and Chandellas (Option 3): Paramaras, Chauhans and Chandellas were Rajput dynasties of Malwa, Ajmer and Bundelkhand who rose later. They were not the three main contenders for Kannauj.

 

• Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas (Option 4): Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas were the three Tamil kingdoms of the far south. They had no part in the Gangetic struggle.
